items.title: Classic triad of nephritic syndrome
items.contentHtml:
Classic triad

  • Hematuria (macroscopic in 30-50% of cases, “meat washing water” color), arterial hypertension due to hydrosaline retention and edema (periorbital in the morning, then decline) constitute the typical presentation of nephritic syndrome.
  • Hypertension arterialis secondary to expansion of the extracellular volume and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system; Its severity correlates with the degree of oliguria.
  • Edema appears when sodium and water retention exceeds 2-3 liters; Its initial periorbital location is due to the laxity of the eyelid subcutaneous tissue.

items.title: Dysmorphic hematuria and blood casts
items.contentHtml:
Dysmorphic hematuria and blood casts

  • dysmorphic hematuria (acanthocytes >5% in urinary sediment) indicates glomerular origin; It is due to deformation of erythrocytes when crossing the damaged glomerular basement membrane.
  • The hematic casts (casts of red blood cells) are pathognomonic of acute glomerulonephritis and confirm intratubular bleeding; Its presence requires ruling out nephritic syndrome.
  • Staining of urinary sediment with phase contrast allows for the identification of acanthocytes; a count >80% of dysmorphic red blood cells has specificity >90% for glomerular disease.

items.title: Oliguria and elevated creatinine
items.contentHtml:
Oliguria and elevated creatinine

  • Oliguria (diuresis <400 mL/day in adults) results from decreased glomerular filtration due to inflammation and occupation of Bowman's space; its duration >1 week predicts a worse prognosis.
  • The elevated serum creatinine reflects an acute drop in the glomerular filtration rate; in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis it typically peaks at 7-10 days and normalizes in 3-4 weeks.
  • The fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) is usually <1% in prerenal oliguria, but in nephritic syndrome it may be <1% or >1% depending on the degree of associated tubular damage.

items.title: Most common cause: poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
items.contentHtml:
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis

  • It is the most common cause of nephritic syndrome in children aged 2-15 years; It occurs 1-3 weeks after pharyngeal or cutaneous infection by Streptococcus pyogenes (nephritogenic serotypes 1, 4, 12, 49). electronic.
  • The diagnosis is supported by elevation of antistreptolysin O (ASO) after pharyngeal infection or anti-DNase B after skin infection; titers >200 IU/mL suggest recent infection.

items.title: Previous streptococcal infection (skin or pharynx)
items.contentHtml:
Previous streptococcal infection

  • A history of streptococcal pharyngitis (1-2 weeks before) or pyoderma (2-4 weeks before) is key to the diagnosis of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
  • Pharyngeal infection by Streptococcus pyogenes serotype 12 has a greater nephritogenic risk; cutaneous culture due to serotypes 49 and 55 is associated with greater latency.
  • Pharyngeal or skin culture may be negative at the onset of kidney symptoms; Therefore, serological markers such as antistreptolysin O and anti-DNase B are used to confirm recent exposure.

items.foco: Low C3 serum supplement in acute phase
items.title: Low C3 serum supplement in acute phase
items.contentHtml:
Low serum C3 complement

  • In poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, serum C3 complement is decreased (<90 mg/dL) in more than 90% of patients during the acute phase, while C4 is usually normal (alternate complement pathway).
  • Normalization of serum complement C3occurs in 6-8 weeks; its low persistence beyond 8 weeks suggests other glomerulonephritis such as lupus nephritis or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.
  • Serial determination of serum complement C3 and C4 helps in the differential diagnosis: in lupus nephritis both are decreased (classical route); in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis only C3.

items.foco: Arterial hypertension due to hydrosaline retention
items.title: Arterial hypertension due to hydrosaline retention
items.contentHtml:
Arterial hypertension due to hydrosaline retention

  • The arterial hypertension in nephritic syndrome is predominantly due to intravascular volume expansion due to sodium and water retention, not due to activation of the renin-angiotensin system.
  • Blood pressure is usually moderately elevated (95th-99th percentile for age); figures >99th percentile +3 standard deviations indicate hypertensive encephalopathy if associated with headache or seizures.
  • Initial management consists of sodium restriction (<2 g/day) and loop diuretics (furosemide 1-2 mg/kg/intravenous dose) to reduce extracellular volume; Beta blockers or angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors are not first line.

items.foco: Morning periorbital edema and lower limbs
items.title: Morning periorbital edema and lower limbs
items.contentHtml:
Morning periorbital edema and lower limbs

  • Morning periorbital edema is characteristic of nephritic syndrome due to nocturnal redistribution of fluid; As the day progresses it moves to lower limbs due to the effect of gravity.
  • The edema is soft, pitted and symmetrical; its intensity is graded from + to ++++ (sinking of 2 mm, 4 mm, 6 mm and 8 mm respectively).
  • In young children, edema may manifest as sudden weight gain (>5% in 1-2 days) before becoming clinically evident; sodium restriction and loop diuretics are the basis of symptomatic treatment.

items.foco: Treatment: sodium restriction and loop diuretics
items.title: Treatment: sodium restriction and loop diuretics
items.contentHtml:
Treatment: sodium restriction and loop diuretics

  • Sodium restriction (<2 g/day) and Loop diuretics (furosemide 1-2 mg/kg/intravenous dose every 6-12 hours) constitute the mainstay of the management of fluid overload and hypertension arterial.
  • The dose of furosemide should be adjusted according to renal function; in glomerular filtration rate <30 mL/min, higher doses are required (up to 4 mg/kg/dose) due to decreased tubular secretion.
  • Loop diuretics are contraindicated if there is uncorrected hypovolemia or hypokalemia; Monitoring electrolytes and daily weight is mandatory to avoid excessive depletion.

items.foco: Indication for kidney biopsy: rapid deterioration or anuria
items.title: Indication for kidney biopsy: rapid deterioration or anuria
items.contentHtml:
Indication of renal biopsy

  • The renal biopsy is indicated in nephritic syndrome in the event of rapid deterioration of renal function (increase in creatinine >50% in 48 hours), anuria (<50 mL/day) or persistence of oliguria >2 weeks.
  • Other indications include low serum C3 complement that does not return to normal within 8 weeks, proteinuria in the nephrotic range (>3.5 g/day), or suspicion of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (presence of crescents in the biopsy).
  • The renal biopsy should be performed with ultrasound control and platelet count. >100,000/μL; major complications (retroperitoneal hematoma, arteriovenous fistula) occur in <1% of cases.

items.foco: Differential diagnosis with rapidly progressive nephritic syndrome
items.title: Differential diagnosis with rapidly progressive nephritic syndrome
items.contentHtml:
Differential diagnosis with rapidly progressive nephritic syndrome

  • The rapidly progressive nephritic syndrome is characterized by loss of kidney function in weeks (increase in creatinine >50% in 3 months) and presence of crescents in >50% of the glomeruli in the renal biopsy.
  • It differs from classic nephritic syndrome due to the speed of deterioration, the absence of a history of streptococcal infection and the need for immunosuppressive treatment (pulse methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3 days plus cyclophosphamide).
  • The causes include granulomatosis with polyangiitis (associated with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies), lupus nephritis class IVand Goodpasture disease (anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies); serology and kidney biopsy are essential.

items.foco: Favorable prognosis in children with poststreptococcal
items.title: Favorable prognosis in children with poststreptococcal
items.contentHtml:
Favorable prognosis in children with poststreptococcal disease

  • In children with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, complete recovery occurs in >95% of cases, with normalization of serum creatinine, disappearance of hematuria (3-6 months) and resolution of proteinuria (1-2 years).
  • Poor prognostic factors: age >40 years, glomerular filtration rate <30 mL/min on admission, persistent nephrotic proteinuria and presence of semilanes >50% in the renal biopsy.
  • Recurrence of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is exceptional if the primary infection is treated; Antibiotic prophylaxis is not required, but contact control with throat culture and carrier treatment is required.
